```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

## Introduction

The safety of a study drug is often monitored while the treatment
assignment of an ongoing trial is still blinded. The blinded data show which
subjects had an adverse event of special interest, but not their treatment
groups. bssd computes the posterior probability that the risk of the event is
higher on the study drug than on placebo from such data, with the models
examined by Duncan (2026):

- BDRIBS(1) and BDRIBS(2), the Poisson-based model of
  Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) with the total exposure time or the total time
  at risk (`bdribs_post()`);
- EXP_BERN, the exponential Bernoulli mixture model (`expbern_post()`);
- LL_BERN, the log-logistic Bernoulli mixture model (`llbern_post()`).

Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) computed the posterior distributions by Markov
chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. bssd computes them by numerical
integration, so the results do not depend on a random seed, and they are fast
enough for simulation studies of the operating characteristics (`sim_oc()`).
The articles `vignette("bdribs1")`, `vignette("bdribs2")`,
`vignette("expbern")` and `vignette("llbern")` describe each model in detail,
with examples, the accuracy of the numerical integration and the comparison
with MCMC.

## Models

The study drug and placebo are randomized in the ratio $k:1$. The prior
distribution of the placebo parameters is based on historical placebo data
with the event rate $\lambda_{HP}$ and the total patient time $PT_{HP}$,
discounted by the factor $DF$.

**BDRIBS.** The number of subjects with the event in the blinded data, $Y$,
follows
$$Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{E \delta (r k + 1) / (k + 1)\},$$
where $E$ is the exposure, $\delta$ is the event rate on placebo and $r$ is
the rate ratio of the study drug to placebo. The priors are
$\delta \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF)$ with
shape and rate parameters, and $r = p / \{k (1 - p)\}$ with
$p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$. BDRIBS(1) uses the total exposure time as $E$.
BDRIBS(2) uses the total time at risk, which leaves out the time after the
first occurrence of the event. Both are computed by `time_at_risk()`.

**EXP_BERN.** Subject $i$ with the follow-up time $t_i$ had the event
($Y_i = 1$) with the probability
$$P(Y_i = 1) = w_p \{1 - \exp(-\lambda_p t_i)\} + w_d \{1 - \exp(-r \lambda_p t_i)\},$$
where $w_p = 1 / (k + 1)$ and $w_d = k / (k + 1)$. The priors of
$\lambda_p$ and $r$ are those of $\delta$ and $r$ in BDRIBS.

**LL_BERN.** The exponential distribution is replaced by the log-logistic
distribution,
$$P(Y_i = 1) = w_p F(t_i; \mu_p, \sigma_p) + w_d F(t_i; \mu_d, \sigma_d), \quad F(t; \mu, \sigma) = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + \exp\{(\log t - \mu) / \sigma\}},$$
so that the hazard can change over time (`ll_cdf()`). The relative risk is
the ratio of the cumulative incidences at a time $t^*$,
$RR(t^*) = F(t^*; \mu_d, \sigma_d) / F(t^*; \mu_p, \sigma_p)$. Duncan (2026)
does not state which relative risk is used for this model. `?llbern_post`
describes this choice and the priors.

A signal is declared when the posterior probability that the relative risk
exceeds the critical value $rr_0$ is larger than a threshold,
$P(RR > rr_0 \mid \mathrm{data}) > \mathrm{cutoff}$. The defaults are
$rr_0 = 1$ and $\mathrm{cutoff} = 0.95$.

## Example with aggregate data

Hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Section 4.4) has a 2:1
randomization, a background event rate of 0.011 per patient-year on placebo,
and 540 patient-years of blinded exposure. The screening analysis of the
article treats the background rate as known, which corresponds to
`pt_hp = Inf`. With the uniform prior for $p$, the posterior probabilities
for 8 and 9 events are

```{r aggregate}
ex2 <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), y = c(8, 9))
ex2$bssd <- mapply(function(y, rr0) {
  bdribs_post(y = y, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011, pt_hp = Inf,
              p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0, details = FALSE)$prob
}, ex2$y, ex2$rr0)
ex2$published <- c(0.622, 0.434, 0.756, 0.584)
knitr::kable(ex2[, c("y", "rr0", "bssd", "published")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Events", "rr0", "bssd", "Mukhopadhyay et al."))
```

The published values were computed by MCMC with the bdribs package, and they
differ from the values of bssd by at most
`r signif(max(abs(ex2$bssd - ex2$published)), 1)`. The print method
summarizes the posterior with 9 events:

```{r aggregate-print}
fit9 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                    pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit9
fit90 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                     pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1), level = 0.90)
```

The posterior mean of $r$ is `r round(fit9$rr[["mean"]], 2)`, and the
article reports 1.53. The article gives (0.52, 2.83) as the 95% interval of
$r$. This agrees with the equal-tailed 90% interval,
(`r round(fit90$rr[["lower"]], 2)`, `r round(fit90$rr[["upper"]], 2)`),
which `level = 0.90` gives, and the equal-tailed 95% interval is
(`r round(fit9$rr[["lower"]], 2)`, `r round(fit9$rr[["upper"]], 2)`).

## Example with subject-level data

The following data are simulated with `sim_blinded()` under the placebo
distribution and the largest study drug distribution of scenario 6 in
Table 1 of Duncan (2026). The 150 subjects are randomized 1:1, they enter the
trial uniformly over 26 weeks, and each subject is followed for up to 104
weeks. The time to the event has a log-logistic distribution with
$\sigma = 0.8$, for which the hazard first increases and then decreases. The
cumulative incidence at week 104 is
`r round(100 * ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 1)`% on placebo and
`r round(100 * ll_cdf(104, mu = 5.85, sigma = 0.8), 1)`% on the study drug.
The blinded analysis is at week 117, the third interim analysis in the
simulations of the folder `reproduce` of the installed package.

```{r subject-data}
set.seed(2026)
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(5.85, 0.8))
head(d[, c("id", "entry", "follow_up", "event", "event_time")])
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
tar
```

The column `group` of `d` holds the true treatment group, which the blinded
analyses do not use.

The priors follow the simulations in the folder `reproduce`: a historical
placebo group of 75 subjects, the size of the current placebo group, followed
for 104 weeks and discounted by $DF = 2$. For BDRIBS and EXP_BERN,
$\lambda_{HP}$ is the constant hazard per week that gives the placebo
incidence at week 104, and $PT_{HP}$ is in patient-weeks. For LL_BERN, the
Gamma priors of $\mu_p$ and $\sigma_p$ have the means `mu_hp` and `sigma_hp`,
and `pt_hp` divided by `df_p` sets their precision. The simulations use the
historical patient time in patient-years for it.

```{r subject-fit}
lambda_hp <- -log(1 - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8)) / 104
pt_weeks <- 75 * 104
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks,
                        df = 2, t_star = 104),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                        t_star = 104),
  EXP_BERN = expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                          lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                          t_star = 104),
  LL_BERN = llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                        sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = pt_weeks / 52, df_p = 2,
                        t_star = 104)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
knitr::kable(res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "ip_placebo",
                     "ip_drug", "ip_difference")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE)
sig <- res$model[res$signal]
```

The column `prob` is $P(RR > 1 \mid \mathrm{data})$. Models with a signal at
the threshold 0.95:
`r if (length(sig) > 0) paste(sig, collapse = ", ") else "none"`. The
relative risk is the rate ratio $r$ for the BDRIBS and EXP_BERN models and
$RR(104)$ for LL_BERN. The table shows its posterior median, because the
posterior mean of $r$ is infinite for EXP_BERN under the default
Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior of $p$ (see `?expbern_post`). The last three columns are
the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 104 and of their
difference. The true values are
`r round(ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 3)`,
`r round(ll_cdf(104, mu = 5.85, sigma = 0.8), 3)` and
`r round(ll_cdf(104, mu = 5.85, sigma = 0.8) - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8), 3)`.

## Accuracy of the numerical integration

`bdribs_post()` integrates over one dimension with `stats::integrate()`.
`expbern_post()` (two dimensions) and `llbern_post()` (four dimensions) use
Gauss-Legendre and Chebyshev quadrature on a region located by a coarse grid.
With `control$check = TRUE`, the default, they repeat the computation on a
finer grid, return the finer result, and report an estimate of the
integration error of `prob`:

```{r error}
vapply(fits[c("EXP_BERN", "LL_BERN")], function(f) f$integration$error,
       numeric(1))
```

The number of nodes can be changed with `control`. `?llbern_post` explains
why the error estimate of LL_BERN is twice the difference between the two
grids. `sim_oc()` turns the check off by default to save time.

## Operating characteristics

`sim_oc()` simulates trials with `sim_blinded()`, applies the selected models
at each analysis, and returns the proportion of trials with a signal and the
posterior mean of the difference in the cumulative incidence. The example
below uses the BDRIBS models with 200 simulated trials to keep the run time
short; the column `se` is the Monte Carlo standard error of `prob_signal`.
The cumulative incidence at week 52 is 10% on placebo and 20% on the study
drug, 350 subjects enter over 26 weeks, and the analyses are at weeks 26, 52
and 78.

```{r oc}
rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
design <- list(n = 350, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
               analysis_time = c(26, 52, 78), dist = "exponential",
               par_p = rate_of(0.10, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.20, 52))
oc <- sim_oc(n_sim = 200, design = design,
             models = c("BDRIBS1", "BDRIBS2"),
             priors = list(bdribs = list(lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52),
                                         pt_hp = 175 * 52, df = 2)),
             t_star = 52, seed = 1)
knitr::kable(oc$summary[, c("analysis_time", "model", "prob_signal", "se",
                            "mean_ip_difference",
                            "mean_observed_difference")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The true difference in the cumulative incidence at week 52 is
`r round(oc$truth[["difference"]], 3)`. The column
`mean_observed_difference` is the mean difference between the proportions of
subjects with the event in the two groups at the analysis, computed from the
true group assignment. The scripts in the folder `reproduce`
(`system.file("reproduce", package = "bssd")`) run the simulations of
Duncan (2026) for all four models with 1000 trials per scenario.

## Reproduction and validation

The installed package contains the scripts and the results of the
reproduction of published results (folder `reproduce`) and of the comparison
with independent computations (folder `validation`). Each item is judged as
PASS (agreement within the tolerance), EXPLAINED (a difference whose reason
is registered), FAIL (a difference without a registered reason) or INFO (no
value to compare with). The numbers of items are

```{r validation, echo = FALSE}
count_judgements <- function(folder, pattern) {
  dir <- system.file(folder, "results", package = "bssd")
  files <- list.files(dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
  rows <- lapply(files, function(f) {
    j <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)$judgement
    n <- table(factor(j, levels = c("PASS", "EXPLAINED", "FAIL", "INFO")))
    data.frame(file = basename(f), PASS = n[["PASS"]],
               EXPLAINED = n[["EXPLAINED"]], FAIL = n[["FAIL"]],
               INFO = n[["INFO"]])
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
judgements <- rbind(count_judgements("reproduce", "^reproduce_.*[.]csv$"),
                    count_judgements("validation", "^validate_.*[.]csv$"))
knitr::kable(judgements, row.names = FALSE)
```

The reproduction covers Table 1, the hypothetical examples and the operating
characteristics of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), and Table 1, Figure 1 and the
simulations of Figures 2 to 10 of Duncan (2026). Many simulation results are
INFO, because the article does not report all settings of the simulations
and the published values are read from the figures. The validation compares
`bdribs_post()` with the bdribs package, `expbern_post()` and `llbern_post()`
with MCMC in JAGS, the default integration grids with finer grids and with an
independent Python implementation, and `sim_oc()` with an independent Python
simulation. The number of FAIL items is `r sum(judgements$FAIL)`. The files
`README.md` and `results/SUMMARY.md` in each folder describe the scripts,
the tolerances and the reasons for the EXPLAINED items.

## References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using
alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. *Journal of
Biopharmaceutical Statistics*, 36(2), 227-244.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532>

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian
detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data.
*Pharmaceutical Statistics*, 17(6), 823-834.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898>
